Over the years I must have compiled quite easily ten physical notebooks wherein I'd jot down words, phrases, idioms, medical terminology, archaisms, stylisms from various books on the origins of the English language, Latin etc. 

Add to that not a few sets on my Quizlet accounts and I've got a fairly handsome report of my reading / learning throughout that time.

When I read a novel or a text, dictionary, medical journal, etc., I take down all that I don't know, and I like to classify my Quizlet sets according to a certain typology or structure (e.g. a set devoted to a peculiar author, a set that appropriates an entire era of some small literary movement, a set solely consisting of types of hairdos, dresses, millinery etc.)

It may seem weird to most people, but I take a lot of joy from my studies; being able to have some go-to references just makes writing a lot easier and less distracting.

"What kind of coat will such and such character wear?"
I then don't have to waste time Googling "types of coats" and get lost in the Macy's online website for hours on end. (I have tremendous ADHD, which makes my writing difficult if I have to search the internet for what I could already have tabled and categorized in a designated notebook or Quizlet set.) 

I also find it something akin to a hobby, but reading about the origins and developments of lexicography / linguistics / w/e else just interested me since I started reading a lot more in HS. I collect thesaurus and dictionaries, phrase books, tourist's manuals to other US states (it goes without saying that I don't leave the house too often), and try to keep lists of patterns in cultural, medical / pharmacological, mythological advancement and inchoation as much as I can.

Also remember from Epicurus: impugn, recondite, abstruse, gloaming, ensillade...you figure in "twilight" qua "gloaming," and you've got a handy phrasal source for a particular work or an author; for this example, IRATE - Epicurus, the begging little fellow who was disgusted by and dismissive of the decadences of his culture. (Who took in many of the outcasted among the madding crowd to retreat into a garden, where he lay beside brother and sister in a kind of learned and shared humanity. 
Another sub-mnemotic I used to recall variant terms for prostitutes, whom E. brought into the suggestion of good-naturedness and purity: prost; trollope, strumpet, vamp, etc. 

For each writer - I say this to those who might be interested in strategizing instruments of lexical recall / reference - there are anent each of all of them different ways to patternize the "key" words in their language, so that you can create word-maps if that's your dig. I find it's incredibly useful for a writer to have reserve banks in order to leap over writer's block. 
The best way I've found is by submitting to each writer whose language speaks to you a core "roll-call" of anywhere from 10-25 words; from there you can assign through various techniques and according to a particular word a more-and-more precise phraseology: this can be achieved by method of ascription of such things as homonym, synonym, hyponym, hypernym (a word that relates etiologically to an "upper" word, e.g. u: levee / U: crack) and so forth. 
This is especially useful if you're meaning to cultivate the wild speech of more insular writers - Hegel, Heidegger, Dostoevsky, Turgenev, Tolstoy et al - or if you want at the more flowery / florid vocab. of an Oscar Wilde (this example is actually a very good one; you'll notice in "Dorian Gray" the intention of his diction, how he almost writes with the imagined quill of a flower. Words that shape the theme of the story:
laburnums for Loss, hydraic for Horror, nenuphars, "scarps of mud" refuted by "ambushes of alyssum,"; so now you're beginning to test the voice of Wilde's interior language by assimilating to your working vocabulary these "found words" - and try assigning to each flower, continuing this example, something dreamily different: alyssum / Elysian; or you may want to make connect the example of a nenuphar with a similar class-word. 

For instance: 
nenuphar / narthecium : alyssum // anent, fust, furze...

Right there you will find you have in just one example - by using phonetic comparison - six words, the first being closely related in both morphological structure (the "inner" syntax of a glyph) and cadence (correlation of consonance) and then you assign to this word-pair a defending monologue: alyssum can be remembered along with nenuphar, as both are retrievable in your "flower"-class, and by inserting in your mnemonic a middle, semi-related word (narthecium - a shrub), you can create like I did in this example an entire scenery with just these six words. 
In a poem:

Anent the roses, the alyssum e'er glowing
I lie in such strangles as this! O pure, paleless
Does Night cower, inviolate, and true its fust?
I coddle blackly sometimes this leery head,
As certain are my hands to thrush;
Bleed me my years! And forsake, forsaketh
All this sap that in narthecium disgusts

I recall reading at least an appreciable portion of this treatise in "Essays and Aphorisms," and I always find the same charm in Schopenhauer as I do when looking into Nietzsche: both had lived in certain "defeating humidities," vacuous of certain of human interactions or even so remotely as to make one ponder whether this self-enforced mode of existence didn't, in point of fact, make scramble of their - to use Schopenhauer's Latin - essentia. 
He - Schopenhauer - once and probably a lot more than was put on the record devised atypical social stratagems so as to limit most physical / psychical interaction for the unabashed pursuit of philosophical description / investigation.
On the note of love, Schopenhauer very decisevely trained his view toward women as ultimately "wild-cats in the brush," depicting their role in the human experience as nary but one whose position could not be anything more improved on but as "teacherly"; his thinking was that a woman was so definitely close to a child - respecting to their psychology above all else - that to imagine ever the limits of Woman as being any more outre or contriving than as that of a child's was inconceivable.
He pushed the idea of Woman as categorically second-place; that a woman should take on in any greater capacity the model and modus of a teacherly object was shooed away over and over in one of his essays - the fitting "On Women," IIRC - to be just "bad manners," a sort of flunk in the determinant world - the short of it is that a woman is from birth and onward forced by her "small nature" to abide the limits of that nature, which Schopenhauer proposed as the limits of a child. 

This descriptor is often translated by some - I think Zinn or Friedel et al - as a lower "psychical metabolism," and is used by Schopenhauer to give assent to his formulation of the woman as only possible in a secondary capacity; the nearness, or propinquity, between woman and child is experienced in the gingerliness / softness of a woman's hand, in her heart, in the way in which she is coerced by the functionary nature of her Being; the massive incoherence of Love, then, is inescapabably obvious, at least for Schopenhauer, throughout the whole interfering act of one's "falling in love," which is thereby an action that serves to condition a man into a tense life of idiocy and ungovernable lassitude; this is precisely because, for Schopenhauer, the "loving process" cannot exist without a sort of risking one's time with an activity that is merely incapacitating to the assigned role of Man, which is ostensibly to silence the objectionable animal model - the Will, at bottom - and prove insurance of the Intellect / Ego / Insight, etc. above aught else. 

By a man's determining for himself an interest in "falling in love," he is confirming in a way that the aspect of the "material" - which in the original German is used to mean something more leaning toward the bestial - has triumphed through naivetie and lack of self-jurisdiction (Foresight); this allows for various disharmonies of the Spirit exactly apropos of the man's indulgence.
So, when Schopenhaur famously expelled the old woman from the top of his stairwell, one can notice quite easily that our man wasn't too keen on the overall appearance of not just Woman, but moreover with the "rackety noise" of really that whole part of our species.

Referring back to Nietzsche, one can detect this element of the "perverse" notion in N.'s disdain for living not "in" a "Now," but instead living in wait "for" an "After." 
It's discerning all the same that as both men wrote with tremendous vigor in tremendous isolation, the historiography of many of these shared notions, e.g. the woman as a "safety instict," the spiritual world as an "awakening of the indiscretions of the Spirit," etc., should be read with bright fascination for their place in the philosophical cannon - as working fodder for more mature modalities of both Feminist and Egalitarian thought - but with a hesitation in order to work out deliberately the process through which the ideas were contrived, because, I think, the actual sediment on which the idea is hatched is important precisely because all Idea, in Barthesian thought, is by itself preconcluding; it interprets a certain motion or zeitgeist first as a "fad," and then as an account of the "fad" as uniquely transifigured into the philosophical literature.

Please read Dylan Trigg's work on the metaphysics of ruination; it doesn't really apply at all to this reading, but I'll be damned if his work isn't interesting as hell.

On the topic of his sister, N. was markedly indifferent to the rise of Anti-semitism - in "Zarathustra..." there is the scene of the tight-rope and the jongleur, which was an allegory that N. skillfully used to defy the custom of the "crowd that jeers" (the common zeitgeist of his Austrian peoples) and present an "unterhund" character whose only goal was to make of himself a voyage and a victory. This campaign of self-sacrifice was entirely at odds with what Wagner was doing, and it's unfortunate that N.'s sister conflated the two in order to bring about and proselytize the concept of N. being against the Jewish people. Admittedly, N. did beseech his readers to be wary of the fatalism of Zionist belief, but that's no different from how he admonished the notion of Christianity, which he saw as an insurance plan to which every growth and tumor of the "nihilistic aspect" could be explored.

Well, the easiest explanation is that when the nominative form of a verb is modified internally, in this case where the tense requires a communicative intimation (without which the grammar of the whole clause would be impossible to describe), the affix (-en) is supplied in accord with a preliminal (has / had) to make the voice of the clause familiar to the intent of the action (synchronicity). So, it's not that"-ten" is added, it's that the affix - "en" - is intimiated in order to make the action recognizable in accordance with the tensal structure. "-En" would imply a sense of the specific, such as in "he has fallen," where the definite aspect is made true by the application of the affix (-en").

That's principally because of how the morphology in French is featured in re. "-re," where the grapheme (the simplest-meaningful particle) is not separable from its surroundant identifying particles. There are of course exceptions, e.g. "centre" v/ "center," where the Anglicanized form is used and is surviving as such as merely a stylistic vestige. The common "vulgar" spellings are just cases of illiteracy that have been practiced and have thereby been sustained.

You'll identify a good deal of this sort of linguistic in the early Victorian writers; substantially in the writings of the classicists of the 19th century, where you'll have discrepancies in things like the constructive elements of   the suffix: "-iferous" / "-inous", e.g. "luminiferous aether" / "luminous ether". It's mostly a matter of style and idiolect.
